name: Epithalamin
lead: Epithalamin is a peptide preparation extracted from the pineal gland of cattle, developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia. The synthetic tetrapeptide Epitalon was later derived from it.[8][9]

Studies from the group report that it lengthened lifespan in fruit flies, mice and rats, and that it raised melatonin production in old rats.[2][4][5] Most evidence is animal data from the same group. No randomized controlled trial in humans was found among the sources reviewed.

paras: A 2002 review states that the group developed a technology for making complex peptide preparations from tissue extracts, including a pineal preparation, Epithalamin, which increased outgrowth of pineal explants and increased melatonin production in rats.[8]

A 1992 study reported an effect on lifespan and on pineal and serum melatonin in old rats.[4] A 1997 Drosophila study compared Epithalamin with melatonin for lifespan and free-radical oxidation.[2] A 1998 paper concluded from fruit-fly, mouse and rat data that Epithalamin increased lifespan.[5] A 1994 review covered twenty years of work in experimental gerontology and oncology.[3] Later papers reported restored hormonal function of pineal gland and pancreas in age-related disturbance[6] and antioxidant properties of pineal peptides.[7] A 2025 review covers Epitalon.[9]

A separate 2003 review discusses the pineal gland's role in breast cancer, noting that pinealectomy or constant light increase mammary carcinogenesis in rodents while light deprivation reduces it.[1] This concerns the gland, not specifically Epithalamin.
No studies found. Findings found are in fruit flies, rodents and reviews by the developing group.[2][3][5][8]

card.summary: The bovine pineal extract behind Epitalon, with lifespan data in flies and rodents but no human trials.
card.note: Animal-derived; data largely from its developers.

quick.overview:
Epithalamin is a pineal-gland peptide extract developed in Russia, from which the tetrapeptide Epitalon was derived.

Animal studies from the developing group report longer lifespan in flies, mice and rats. It has no documented appearance use and no randomized human trial was found.
quick.mechanism: Proposed actions include raising pineal melatonin output and antioxidant effects; these are reported in animals.
quick.risks: Human safety data was not found in the sources reviewed. It is an animal-derived preparation not approved in most countries.
